title: Diagnostic expansion: Institutions reshaped recognized autism
desc: Explains rising diagnosis through reorganized expertise, measurement, care and advocacy, while separating institutional scalability from therapeutic efficacy.

kps.k: The cluster explains expanding autism diagnosis through the reorganization of expertise, care and diagnostic categories.
kps.d: In For a Sociology of Expertise: The Social Origins of the Autism Epidemic, the author asks why autism previously remained rare rather than treating rising diagnoses as a self-explanatory increase in underlying prevalence. The article challenges natural-cause accounts and argues that invoking medicalization or broader criteria still leaves their historical emergence unexplained. Its substantive proposition combines professional jurisdiction with the networks, tools and cooperation that make diagnosis possible at scale.

qs.q: Instead of asking why autism is more prevalent now, I suggest that we ask first why autism was rare in the past.
qs.a: For a Sociology of Expertise: The Social Origins of the Autism Epidemic · Academia · 2013

qs.q: If changed diagnostic criteria are the proximate cause, for example, the question obviously becomes why were they changed?
qs.a: For a Sociology of Expertise: The Social Origins of the Autism Epidemic · Academia · 2013

kps.k: Deinstitutionalization and parent–professional collaboration made autism more distinguishable and diagnosis more scalable.
kps.d: The author identifies deinstitutionalization from the early 1970s over at least two decades as a key historical mechanism. Custodial institutions had little reason to distinguish autism from intellectual disability; family care, special education and community services made communication and interaction actionable concerns. Parents resisted stigmatizing clinical accounts and exchanged information with psychologists and therapists through checklists, newsletters and home observations. The argument distinguishes weakening psychiatrists' monopoly from weakening expertise: distributing knowledge and decisions could expand capacity and cooperation without turning parents into another profession.

qs.q: This is why I will argue that the deinstitutionalization of mental retardation—a lengthy process that began in the early 1970s and lasted at least two decades—was a key cause leading to the autism epidemic.
qs.a: For a Sociology of Expertise: The Social Origins of the Autism Epidemic · Academia · 2013

qs.q: Thus, deinstitutionalization created a changed institutional terrain in which the family, surrounded by support services, became the preferred locus for the diagnosis and treatment of children with developmental disabilities.
qs.a: For a Sociology of Expertise: The Social Origins of the Autism Epidemic · Academia · 2013

kps.k: Measurement tools and therapeutic practices helped reshape what clinicians and families recognized as autism.
kps.d: Observation screens and parent-facing checklists exposed clinical work to scrutiny and supported standardized observation. The article reports Rimland's finding that only 55 of 445 children seen by two clinicians received matching diagnoses, and links reliability concerns to psychiatry's adoption of measurement tools. It also argues that individualized therapies reframed autism as separately actionable behaviors and a spectrum of social and communicative difficulties. Historical illustrations include changes in self-injury's diagnostic status across DSM editions and broader reciprocal-interaction criteria. These examples support the author's account of changing classification, not a direct measurement of changes in underlying prevalence.

qs.q: Using them, he was able to show that out of 445 children who saw two different clinicians only 55 received the same diagnosis (Rimland 1971, pp.
qs.a: For a Sociology of Expertise: The Social Origins of the Autism Epidemic · Academia · 2013

qs.q: Ultimately, psychiatry would incorporate these into its arsenal, especially with the DSM-III (1980), which was explicitly designed to guarantee diagnostic reliability in response to studies like Rimland’s demonstrating lack of agreement among clinicians.
qs.a: For a Sociology of Expertise: The Social Origins of the Autism Epidemic · Academia · 2013

kps.k: The account separates therapies' organizational success from evidence of clinical efficacy.
kps.d: The author attributes therapeutic diffusion to individualized goals, integration into family and school routines, and the ability to enlist parents and children—not demonstrated technical superiority. The contrast with hospitalization-based childhood schizophrenia treatment emphasizes the loss of cooperation when promised cures failed. Participation was not necessarily voluntary or benign: the article also describes intensive, intrusive treatment and resistance. Its practical implication is to examine how services sustain cooperation while assessing clinical effectiveness separately; the therapeutic anecdotes do not establish efficacy or justify treatment recommendations.

qs.q: The success and spread of these therapies, therefore, was not due to their technical superiority but to the propitious ecology provided by deinstitutionalization and the social innovativeness with which they were able to graft themselves onto the practices of parents and patients, translate their interests, and secure their cooperation.
qs.a: For a Sociology of Expertise: The Social Origins of the Autism Epidemic · Academia · 2013

qs.q: Put differently, because the treatment of childhood schizophrenia emulated the medical model of acute care—hospitalization-treatment-discharge—securing the cooperation of patients and parents was completely staked upon obtaining a “cure,” and when it failed to materialize the initial begrudging cooperation turned into open resistance.
qs.a: For a Sociology of Expertise: The Social Origins of the Autism Epidemic · Academia · 2013

kps.k: Self-advocacy reinforced autism's broader public meaning while creating conflict over cure and representation.
kps.d: The author accepts Hacking's account of memoirs and testimony making autistic people's inner lives publicly intelligible, but asks what enabled self-advocates to emerge. The proposed explanation combines spectrum expansion, participatory therapies and disability-rights organizing, while acknowledging individual advocates' exceptional achievements. The article reports tension between advocates rejecting cure and parents who viewed neurodiversity claims as neglecting severe disability. It also argues that parent organizations helped establish advocates' credibility despite these disagreements.

qs.q: I find Hacking’s argument extremely insightful, yet it leaves completely unexplained the appearance of the self-advocates themselves.
qs.a: For a Sociology of Expertise: The Social Origins of the Autism Epidemic · Academia · 2013

qs.q: Perhaps the most obvious point is that if autism had remained a relatively rare disorder and had not been transformed by the therapies into a spectrum accommodating different levels of severity, it is highly unlikely that the self-advocates would have been recognized as autistic, and their testimony would not have been taken as relevant.
qs.a: For a Sociology of Expertise: The Social Origins of the Autism Epidemic · Academia · 2013

kps.k: Diagnostic substitution and accretion connect the historical mechanisms to recorded growth, but their contribution remains qualified.
kps.d: The author argues that available therapies, expectations of unrealized potential, parental expertise and community-based goals encouraged adding autism diagnoses or substituting them for intellectual-disability diagnoses. The article reports agreement that these processes explained a sizable portion of diagnostic growth during the 1990s, alongside competing estimates; the supplied material establishes no single proportion. Its evidence consists primarily of historical secondary sources, organizational archives and parent-generated accounts. Contemporary interviews and observations informed the inquiry but were not systematically reported. The contribution therefore offers a historical interpretation and a method for studying diagnostic change, rather than a new prevalence estimate or a demonstrated explanation of all diagnostic growth.

qs.q: There are various and competing estimates, yet also agreement, that during the 1990s a sizable portion of the growth in autism diagnoses could be directly imputed to diagnostic accretion and substitution from mental retardation (Shattuck 2006; Coo et al.
qs.a: For a Sociology of Expertise: The Social Origins of the Autism Epidemic · Academia · 2013

qs.q: The data it draws upon are primarily historical and consist of secondary sources about the treatment of mental retardation, autism, and childhood schizophrenia in the United States from 1943—when autism was first reported—to the present.
qs.a: For a Sociology of Expertise: The Social Origins of the Autism Epidemic · Academia · 2013

vlens.an: The supplied academia-and-research source directly accepts the proposition that rising recognized autism diagnoses should be explained through historical changes in institutions, expertise networks, care arrangements, measurement, therapies and advocacy, rather than assumed to reflect a self-explanatory rise in underlying prevalence. Its main reasons are that deinstitutionalization moved diagnosis and intervention into families, schools and community services; parent–professional networks redistributed knowledge and expanded diagnostic capacity; standardized tools changed reliability and classification; therapies helped recast autism as a spectrum of actionable behaviours; and advocacy contributed to autism’s broader public meaning and diagnostic attractiveness. The source also supports the proposition’s distinction between organizational scalability and clinical efficacy: it argues that therapies spread because they secured cooperation and fitted emerging care arrangements, not because their technical superiority had been demonstrated. Material qualification remains within this supportive position: the account is principally historical, does not quantify how much of total diagnostic growth these mechanisms explain, acknowledges competing estimates of diagnostic substitution, and does not systematically report its contemporary interview and observational data. Because only one curated source is supplied for this professional voice, this position should not be generalized to academia or research as a whole.

qs.q: Instead of asking why autism is more prevalent now, I suggest that we ask first why autism was rare in the past.
qs.a: For a Sociology of Expertise: The Social Origins of the Autism Epidemic · Academia · 2013

qs.q: The success and spread of these therapies, therefore, was not due to their technical superiority but to the propitious ecology provided by deinstitutionalization and the social innovativeness with which they were able to graft themselves onto the practices of parents and patients, translate their interests, and secure their cooperation.
qs.a: For a Sociology of Expertise: The Social Origins of the Autism Epidemic · Academia · 2013

elens.an: The pre-2015 source supports the proposition by explaining rising recognized autism diagnoses as the outcome of historical changes in institutions, expertise, measurement, care and advocacy rather than as a self-explanatory rise in underlying prevalence. It identifies deinstitutionalization, parent–professional information networks, standardized diagnostic tools, therapeutic practices, spectrum expansion, self-advocacy, and diagnostic accretion or substitution as mutually reinforcing mechanisms that made autism more identifiable and diagnosable at scale. It also supports the proposition’s distinction between institutional scalability and clinical efficacy: therapies could spread because they organized cooperation across families, schools and professionals without thereby demonstrating technical superiority. Material qualification comes from the evidence base and scope rather than opposition to the proposition: the account is primarily historical, does not systematically report its contemporary research, does not quantify how much of all diagnostic growth these mechanisms explain, and notes internal conflicts over treatment, cure and neurodiversity. Because this period contains one curated source, these findings characterize that source rather than the prevalence of a view among pre-2015 authors.
